It’s strange, being surrounded by such domestic bustle for nearly a week. The Kettle was a necessary anchor when the snow threatened to drift into oblivion, a safe place to wait out the storm while keeping Buttons fed and myself provisioned. I feel sharper now; my patience has been tested in ways that weren't related to tracking or archery. Watching Gerda manage the chaos, seeing how quickly she anticipates needs—it’s a different kind of mastery entirely.

The cost, though... The silver feels thin. It was meant to be a bridge to the next step, not a drain on my reserves. I traded my time, and frankly, some of my sleep, for warmth and shelter. But I learned more about human patience and routine in those few days than I have in all my solitary treks through Highwater's woods.

I need to find work that aligns with *my* strengths—survival, nature’s rhythms, the skills my parents hoped I would perfect. The innkeeper’s life is stable, yes, but it doesn't sharpen the edge of a ranger. My goal isn't simply to survive; it's to become proficient enough to teach others how to thrive in these wild lands.

The road is open now. I must be meticulous about my next move. Where can my skills prove themselves most valuable without demanding months of servitude? A patrol, perhaps, or a specialized guide contract near the grasslands? The family letters are on hand; perhaps it's time to make a more deliberate effort to contact one of them—to Rorie, maybe, who lives near Goldwise and where I might find opportunities that suit my reputation.

I need coin for proper reprovisioning, yes, but more than that, I need clarity on the next stage of this journey. The storm has passed; now begins the real work of charting a course forward.

Stable-lad, server, wood hauler.

The road required me to be self-sufficient; the inn forced me to be indispensable. I am still Misty, the girl who seeks mastery, but perhaps today, that mastery includes knowing how to contribute when the grand plan falls apart.

The journey continues tomorrow, of course. The road waits for no one. *(Misty stands outside the warm glow of the Kettle’s windows, adjusting the cinch on Buttons' saddle. The snow has stopped, and the crisp, cold air carries the scent of pine and thawing earth—the smell of movement once more. She runs a gloved hand over her cloak, feeling its sturdy wool.)*

The map in my head showed a clean line: Highwater to Goldwise, then onward through the grasslands. A direct path toward opportunity, coin, and practice with the bow until my name was known enough that Uncle Bram might even hear of me. The plan was elegant—efficient. Focused purely on measurable progress and skill refinement.

But elegance doesn't account for a stubborn mountain storm. 

I spent four days in an inn, not as a traveler seeking passage, but as a function within it. I traded my freedom for the rhythm of daily necessity: muck, wood-carrying, serving hot stew to strangers who were just as lost and cold as I had been. It was never intended to be this thorough—this *deep*.

My training taught me how to move silently through the underbrush, how to read the signs of a coming squall, how to make an arrow fly true in a gale. But The Kettle taught me something quieter: that self-mastery isn't just about being skilled when things are perfect; it’s about maintaining meticulous standards—keeping the stables clean even when Gerda is stretched thin, keeping my word when I say I will help, and finding efficiency not just in the hunt, but in the simplest routine.

I was looking for a place to *prove* myself as an archer or survivalist to a powerful family. Instead, I proved myself reliable—a steady pair of hands that could be trusted with both heavy water casks and a hot dinner rush.

The road is open now. The delay has cost me days of travel and several precious coins, but perhaps it bought something more valuable than speed: perspective. A ranger must know the wild, yes, but they must also understand the small, stubborn mechanisms that hold human life together. I am not simply leaving a job; I am carrying a new understanding of diligence with me.

Time to saddle up. The road waits for no one.
